mcqs.question: A process requests 4097 bytes on a system with 4 KB pages. How much internal fragmentation does this allocation cause?
options: None — the allocator gives exactly 4097 bytes
About 4095 bytes wasted in the second page
About 4 KB wasted, since one full page is always lost
It depends on how many other processes are running
mcqs.explanation: 4097 bytes needs two 4 KB pages (8192 bytes total); the process uses 4097 of those, leaving 8192 - 4097 = 4095 bytes allocated but unused inside the second page. Allocation is always in whole pages, and this waste doesn't depend on other processes.

mcqs.question: According to Knuth's 50% rule, what does heavy allocate/free churn under first-fit allocation predict?
options: Roughly one unusable hole forms for every two currently-allocated blocks
Fragmentation only depends on total memory size, not on how many allocations occurred
External fragmentation stays constant regardless of allocation activity
Fixed partitioning is immune to this effect
mcqs.explanation: The 50% rule predicts about N/2 additional unusable holes for every N allocated blocks under first-fit, meaning fragmentation grows with allocation churn, not just memory size. Fixed partitioning doesn't have this dynamic-hole behavior at all since its partitions don't split or merge.

mcqs.question: Why does external fragmentation not apply to page frames the way it applies to contiguous variable-size allocation?
options: Page frames are all the same fixed size, so any free frame satisfies any request that needs one frame — there's no notion of an odd-sized unusable gap
Page tables physically compact memory automatically
Because pages are always allocated contiguously in physical memory
Because operating systems reserve extra memory specifically to prevent it
mcqs.explanation: Because every page frame is the same fixed size, a request for N frames just needs N free frames anywhere — no frame can be an oddly-sized unusable sliver. Pages don't need to be physically contiguous, page tables don't compact anything, and no special reserve is required for this property.

mcqs.question: A system reports 2 GB of free memory under contiguous variable-size allocation, but a 1 GB allocation request fails. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The OS's free-memory counter is buggy
The 2 GB is scattered across many holes, none of which is individually close to 1 GB
The request is being blocked by a permissions error unrelated to memory
Free memory can only be allocated in fixed 512 MB chunks
mcqs.explanation: This is the classic external-fragmentation trap: total free bytes can be a correct, non-buggy number while no single hole is big enough for the request, because the space is scattered. There's no fixed 512 MB chunk rule, and nothing here points to a permissions issue.

mcqs.question: Linux's buddy allocator manages physical page frames specifically to keep larger contiguous runs of frames available. Why is this still necessary if paging already eliminated external fragmentation?
options: It isn't necessary — this is a legacy component with no current purpose
Some kernel needs (DMA buffers, huge pages) require physically contiguous multi-frame regions, and frames can still fragment relative to that larger unit
It exists only to speed up single-page allocations
Paging never actually eliminated external fragmentation in the first place
mcqs.explanation: Paging eliminates external fragmentation for single-frame allocations, but some kernel needs require several physically contiguous frames at once, and those larger contiguous runs can still fragment — hence the buddy allocator. It's an active, necessary component, and paging did solve the single-frame case.
